ta-l1d36q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 36 turns to the ideas and announces three articles: whether there are ideas, whether there are several, and whether there are ideas of all things in God.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that there are no ideas. The Philosopher says calling ideas exemplars is empty talk and poetic metaphor, and we call ideas exemplars of things.
claims: Aristotle rejects ideas as exemplars.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e115.summary: Second argument. An agent that needs no exemplar is more perfect than one that does, and God is a perfect agent, so he needs no ideas ('what need is there to look to ideas?', the Philosopher).
claims: A perfect agent needs no exemplar.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e120.summary: Third argument. A thing is better known by its essence than by its likeness (Augustine), and God knows things most nobly, so by their essences, not by ideal likenesses.
claims: Knowledge by essence is better than by likeness.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e124.summary: Fourth argument. Knowledge through a medium is collative and discursive, and God knows by simple intuition.
claims: Mediated knowledge is discursive.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e127.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: whoever denies the ideas denies the Son, which is heretical.
claims: Denying ideas denies the Son.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e133.summary: Second sed contra. The Commentator (Metaphysics 11) says as all forms are potentially in prime matter, they are actually in the first mover, and ideas are the forms of things existing in God.
claims: Forms are actually in the first mover.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e136.summary: Thomas's determination. As artificial forms have twofold being, in act in matter and in active potency in the artisan's mind, so material forms have twofold being (Commentator, Metaphysics 11): in act in things and in active potency in the movers of the orbs, as he holds, and chiefly in the first mover, in whose place we say God. So all philosophers commonly say all things are in God's mind as artefacts in the artisan's, and the forms of things in God are called ideas, as operative forms; Dionysius calls the exemplars the substance-making concepts of beings pre-existing uniformly in God, which theology calls predefinitions and divine and good wills predetermining and producing beings. Yet through the ideas God has not only practical but speculative knowledge of things, since he knows them not only as going out from him but as subsisting in their own natures. 'Idea' comes from 'eidos', form, so by the name's propriety it relates equally to practical and speculative knowledge, since the form of a thing in the intellect is principle of both; though usage takes 'idea' for the principle of practical knowledge, calling the exemplar forms ideas, it is also principle of speculative knowledge, as the contemplated forms of things.
claims: Ideas are the forms of things in God's mind, as artefacts in the artisan's.
Through the ideas God has both practical and speculative knowledge.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e142.summary: Reply to the first argument. As the Commentator says, Plato and the ancients, as if compelled by truth, tended toward what Aristotle later expressed, without reaching it, so Plato in positing ideas tended toward their being in the divine intellect, as Aristotle held; the Philosopher intends to reject not this but Plato's positing natural forms existing by themselves without matter.
claims: Aristotle rejects separate Forms, not ideas in the divine intellect.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e145.summary: Reply to the second argument. If God needed to look to an exemplar outside himself he would be an imperfect agent, but not if his essence is the exemplar of all things, since by beholding his essence he produces all things.
claims: God's essence is the exemplar.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e149.summary: Reply to the third argument. That by which a thing is known must be united to the knower, so created essences, separate from God, cannot be his medium of knowing them; he knows them by a nobler medium, his essence, more perfectly, since then nothing but his essence is the principle of his knowledge, whereas knowing through things' essences would make something else its principle.
claims: God knows things through his essence, a nobler medium than their essences.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e152.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Knowledge is discursive when one goes from what is known to the unknown, not when a thing is grasped by its likeness, or an eye seeing a stone would know collatively. So though God knows things by the likeness in him as medium and knows their order, his knowledge is not discursive, since he beholds all at once.
claims: Knowing through a likeness is not discursive.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e164.summary: First argument that there are not several ideas. An idea is the likeness by which a thing is known, and God knows all by his one essence.
claims: One essence, one idea.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e167.summary: Second argument, against plurality by different respects. God's relations to creatures are really in creatures, not in God, and creatures were not eternal, so neither were these relations or a plurality of ideas, and God knows things now as before he made them (Augustine), so he knows them by one idea.
claims: God's relations to creatures are not eternal.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e170.summary: Third argument. An idea relates to its thing as the art-form to the artefact, and the diversity of artefacts comes from the plurality of forms in the artisan, not conversely, so the diversity of things cannot cause plurality of ideas.
claims: Forms cause artefacts' diversity, not conversely.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e174.summary: Fourth argument. As an idea is relative to the ideated, knowledge is relative to the knowable, and God's knowledge is one though the known are many, so there is one idea of all things.
claims: Knowledge is one despite many objects.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e177.summary: Sed contra. What has no plurality cannot be co-signified in the plural, and Augustine names ideas in the plural: stable concepts of things in the divine mind, which neither arise nor perish, by which all that arises and perishes is made.
claims: Augustine speaks of ideas in the plural.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e180.summary: Second sed contra. Difference causes number (Damascene), and God created man and horse by different concepts (Augustine).
claims: Man and horse have different concepts in God.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e183.summary: Thomas's determination. Since God has proper knowledge of each thing, his essence must be the likeness of singulars, as different things imitate it differently and particularly according to their capacity, though it offers itself as wholly imitable; that creatures imitate it imperfectly and diversely comes from their diversity and defect (Dionysius). Since 'idea' names the divine essence as exemplar imitated by a creature, the essence is the proper idea of a thing according to a determinate mode of imitation, and since different creatures imitate it differently, the idea or concept by which man is created differs from that of horse, so there is plurality of ideas by respect to many things imitating the one essence differently. For example (Dist. 2), every perfection in things belongs to God by one indivisible being: being, living, understanding. All creatures imitate the essence in being, not all in living, and those imitating it in being participate being differently, so the essence has different respects to what has only being, to what has being and life, and to what has being in different ways, and so there are many ideal concepts, as God understands his essence as imitable in this or that way. The understood concepts or modes of imitation are the ideas, since 'idea' names form as understood, not as in the nature of the understander.
claims: Ideas are the divine essence understood as imitable in different determinate ways.
There are many ideas because God understands his one essence as imitable in many ways.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e186.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Idea' names not the essence simply but the essence as imitable, so by the manifold imitability of the divine essence, from the fullness of its perfection, there is a plurality of ideas.
claims: Idea is the essence as imitable.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e189.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though God's relations to creatures are really founded in creatures, they are also in God conceptually and in understanding, not only human but angelic and divine, so though creatures were not eternal, the divine intellect eternally understood its essence as imitable by creatures in various ways, so there was an eternal plurality of ideas in the divine intellect, not in his nature. The form of a horse is in God only as an understood concept, but the concept of life is in God not only as understood but as established in the nature of the thing.
claims: The plurality of ideas is eternal, in God's intellect, not in his nature.
concepts: form of horse vs. life in God

ta-l1d36q2-d1e193.summary: Reply to the third argument. Though the plurality of ideas follows respects to things, the plurality of things does not cause it but the reverse: God's intellect does not behold his essence as variously imitable because things imitate it variously, but the reverse, since the divine intellect causes things and the distinction of ideal concepts follows its operation, as it understands its essence as variously imitable.
claims: The plurality of ideas causes, and is not caused by, the plurality of things.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e196.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The divine essence is one and the respects many, so what names only the essence, like 'knowledge', which holds on the side of the knower as its form, cannot be signified plurally. 'Ratio' holds more on the side of the thing and can be signified plurally ('many concepts'). 'Idea' is midway, implying essence and the concept of imitation, which is a respect, so though plurality is co-signified in it when said in the plural, it is rarely or never signified by adding a numeral ('many ideas'), since plurality is expressed more by signifying than by co-signifying.
claims: 'Scientia' is singular, 'ratio' plural, 'idea' intermediate.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e208.summary: First argument that there are not ideas of all God knows. God knows evils, but there can be no idea of evil, since idea implies imitation and a thing is evil by departing from imitation of God.
claims: No idea of evil.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e211.summary: Second argument. 'Idea' names form, and prime matter has no form, as the first act has no matter.
claims: Prime matter has no form.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e214.summary: Third argument. God knows particulars, but there seems to be no idea of particulars as such, since all singulars of a species share one form.
claims: Singulars share their species' form.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e218.summary: Fourth argument. An idea belongs to what participates it by imitation, and accidents, not subsisting, participate nothing but are participations.
claims: Accidents do not participate.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e221.summary: Sed contra. All knowledge is by a species of the known in the knower, and the species of things in God are called ideas.
claims: Ideas are God's species of all he knows.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e224.summary: Thomas's determination. As Dionysius shows, an idea is the likeness or concept of a thing in God as productive and determinative of it, so each thing has an idea in God as it is related to being produced by God. Whatever is produced by a per se agent imitates it in what it receives from it, since like produces like (the Philosopher), in voluntary and natural agents. So as something is produced by God it has its likeness in him, its idea is in him, and it is known by him, and since all things are produced by God, there are ideas of all things in him.
claims: There are ideas of all things in God, as all are produced by him and like produces like.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e227.summary: Reply to the first argument. Evil as evil is nothing, a privation like blindness, so there is an idea in God of an evil thing not as evil but as a thing, and evil itself is known by God through the opposite good from which the thing subject to privation falls short.
claims: Evil things have ideas as things; evil is known through good.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e230.summary: Reply to the second argument. Since prime matter is from God its idea must be in him somehow, attributed as being is attributed to it, since all being, as perfect, is drawn exemplarily from divine being. Perfect being belongs to matter not in itself but in the composite; in itself it has imperfect being, the last grade, being in potency. So it has the perfect character of idea only in the composite, where God gives it perfect being, and considered in itself an imperfect character of idea: the divine essence is imitable by the composite by perfect being, by matter by imperfect being, by privation in no way. So the composite by its form has a perfect idea in God, matter an imperfect one, privation none.
claims: Composites have perfect ideas, matter imperfect ones, privation none.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e233.summary: Reply to the third argument. Particulars have proper ideas in God, so the concept of Peter differs from that of Martin as man's from horse's. But man and horse differ by form, to which an idea perfectly corresponds, while singulars of one species are distinguished by matter, which does not perfectly have an idea, so the distinction of concepts corresponding to species is more perfect than to individuals, the imperfection belonging to the imitating things, not the imitated essence.
claims: Singulars have proper ideas, less perfectly distinguished than species' ideas.

ta-l1d36q2-d1e237.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Accidents also lack perfect being and so fall short of the perfection of idea, which is why Plato posited ideas only of substances (Metaphysics 1). Yet as they have being by imitating the divine essence, the essence is their idea. This answers the objections and the text.
claims: Accidents have ideas imperfectly.

ta-l1d36q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces three articles on the ideas: whether they exist, whether they are many, and whether there are ideas of all things.

ta-l1d36q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that there are ideas, the forms of things in God's mind as artefacts in the artisan's, the principle of both practical and speculative knowledge. Aristotle rejected separate Forms, not ideas in the divine intellect; God's essence is the exemplar; he knows through his essence, a nobler medium than things' essences; and knowledge through a likeness is not discursive.
claims: Ideas exist as the forms of things in God's mind.

ta-l1d36q2-Dd1e156.summary: Article 2 holds that there are many ideas, since an idea is the divine essence understood as imitable in a determinate way, and God understands his one essence as imitable in many ways. The plurality is eternal, in his intellect not his nature, and causes rather than follows the plurality of things. 'Idea' is midway between the singular 'knowledge' and the plural 'ratio'.
claims: Ideas are many as the essence is understood as variously imitable.

ta-l1d36q2-Dd1e200.summary: Article 3 holds that there are ideas of all things God produces, since like produces like. Evil things have ideas as things, evil being known through good. Composites have perfect ideas, matter imperfect ones, and privation none. Singulars have proper ideas, though less perfectly distinguished than species', and accidents have ideas imperfectly.
claims: There are ideas of all produced things, with grades of perfection.

ta-l1d36q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 36 treats the divine ideas. Article 1 holds that ideas exist as the forms of things in God's mind, principles of practical and speculative knowledge, and that Aristotle rejected only separate Forms. Article 2 holds that there are many ideas, the essence understood as imitable in many ways, eternally in God's intellect and causing the diversity of things. Article 3 holds that there are ideas of all things he produces, perfect for composites and imperfect for matter, singulars, and accidents, with none for privation.
claims: Ideas are the divine essence understood as variously imitable.
There are ideas of all things God produces.
